title: New rule HAL-06: legacy SDK APIs that no longer exist (for example openai<1.0 style calls) (patsypppe/slopaudit)
raw_text:
New rule HAL-06: legacy SDK APIs that no longer exist (for example openai<1.0 style calls) — open-source issue in patsypppe/slopaudit. Labels: help wanted, rules, advanced, rule: LLM, rule: HAL. ## Why
Models trained on older code still write `openai.ChatCompletion.create(...)` and `openai.Completion.create`, which were removed in openai 1.0, and old LangChain import paths. The code looks right and fails at runtime.

## What to do
1. Build a small, documented table of removed APIs per package and version (cite each changelog).
2. Add the rule with `status="experimental"` and an honest severity and confidence; compare against the version declared in the manifest when available.
3. Start
summary:
This open-source issue highlights a common problem where large language models (LLMs), often trained on older code, generate calls to deprecated application programming interfaces (APIs). For example, they might suggest `openai.ChatCompletion.create` which was removed in `openai` version 1.0. While the code looks correct, it fails at runtime because the functions no longer exist. This issue proposes a new rule for `slopaudit` to detect such legacy API calls.

This matters because as you work with LLMs for code generation, you'll inevitably encounter situations where the generated code is outdated. Understanding API versioning and handling deprecations is crucial for building robust LLM-powered applications. It also shows the challenge of keeping LLMs aligned with rapidly evolving library ecosystems.

One thing you could try is to always verify the API versions of libraries when using LLM-generated code. If you see runtime errors about missing functions, check the official documentation for recent API changes.
why: LLMs generate outdated API calls, causing runtime errors; you need to know this.

title: Docs: tutorial for securing a FastAPI + OpenAI chatbot (patsypppe/slopaudit)
raw_text:
Docs: tutorial for securing a FastAPI + OpenAI chatbot — open-source issue in patsypppe/slopaudit. Labels: documentation, help wanted, good first issue. ## Why
A second end-to-end tutorial (next to the LangChain one in #13) for the most common stack: a FastAPI endpoint that calls an LLM.

## What to do
1. Start from a small, deliberately unsafe app: request data in the system prompt, model output rendered or executed, a hardcoded key, no token cap.
2. Scan, explain each finding, fix it, rescan to clean, add the GitHub Action.
3. Run every command and paste real output.

## Where
New `docs/tutorial-fastapi.md`, linked from `docs/README.md`.

## D
summary: This item describes an open-source task to create a tutorial on securing a chatbot built with FastAPI and OpenAI. It aims to guide you through the process of identifying and fixing common security vulnerabilities in such applications. The idea is to start with a deliberately insecure setup – perhaps with hardcoded keys, data in system prompts, or no token limits – and then systematically scan for issues, explain each finding, and implement fixes. This is incredibly important because deploying AI models, especially LLMs, in production requires robust security. You could focus on understanding how prompt injection or insecure API key handling can compromise your application, which are common pitfalls in LLM-powered systems.
why: Learn to secure FastAPI + OpenAI chatbots, crucial for full-stack and MLOps.

title: Show HN: I'm killing AI slop spam with a simple Google script
author: apparent
summary:
this news item describes a founder's simple google script to combat the increasing amount of 'ai slop spam' – unsolicited, low-quality emails clearly generated by ai that google's spam filter often misses. the script helps filter these out, preventing constant phone notifications from irrelevant messages.

this matters because it highlights a practical, real-world challenge emerging from the widespread use of generative ai. while ai creates many benefits, it also enables misuse, like generating spam. understanding this problem is important for anyone working with ai, as it touches on ethical considerations and the need for robust detection mechanisms. you could think about how you might design a system to detect ai-generated text more effectively.
why: shows the real-world problem of ai-generated spam and the need for detection.
